plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) and food: which eating habits and food choices may ease the common stomach side effects (nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, heartburn and burping), why slower stomach emptying makes meal size, fat and pace matter, and when symptoms mean calling a prescriber
plan.angle:
Broad Lane A long video (log 'lane: A'; publisher adds it to 'Life on Tirzepatide'). Runs 9–11 min at 14:00 ET. Evergreen, with no date or holiday words.

Opening:
- Sentence 1 names tirzepatide and the viewer's question, then gives a short answer by 15 s: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping at comfortably full and going easier on greasy food are the habits experts suggest most often.
- Next comes a 'you' scenario: a rich dinner sits like a brick.
- At 15–30 s, give the second concrete payoff: the label's pooled nausea rate per dose vs placebo, plus the label's wording that GI effects happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time. Never shorten that timing to 'first weeks'.

Chapters, each named as a searched question:
1. Why does food feel different on tirzepatide? Use the label's delayed-gastric-emptying wording.
2. What to eat when you're nauseous. Credit only what the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory says ('avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment', at exactly that scope; smaller, more frequent meals). Bland options and eating slowly are untagged tips.
3. Foods for diarrhoea, and fluids. Sip fluids unless you've been told to limit them. Use the label's dehydration and kidney wording, and tag the NHS dehydration signs to NHS.
4. Foods for constipation. Build fibre up gradually with fluids, and explain why that doesn't conflict with the 'first few days' advice.
5. Heartburn and burping. NHS reflux advice goes in only as NHS prints it. 'Sulfur burps' is called a commonly described symptom, with no cause given.
6. Protein when appetite is low. Include the kidney caveat.
7. When to call. Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, means stop and call your healthcare provider right away. Signs of dehydration or vomiting you can't keep up with means contact your prescriber. Then: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.'

Rules:
- All habits are 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'.
- Give label rates with both arms and name the pooled-trial population. Mounjaro rates only if labelled as type 2 diabetes trials.
- Add the low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea.
- No foods called 'bad', no calorie talk, no products, doses or titration.
- Land a payoff before the ~70 s chapter change. Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the chapter 2–4 payoff. Start the end ask at about 85%.
- Include 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
- End with: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.'
- Publisher: line-1 ▶ Watch next link to Side Effects.
- Thumbnail: 4 words or fewer that keep the gap, e.g. 'Which Foods Help?', with one calm, labelled tummy character. No body imagery.

package.description:
▶ Watch next: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Side Effects: [Side Effects video URL]
Smaller meals, eaten slowly, stopping at comfortably full and going easier on greasy food are commonly recommended habits, not results proven in tirzepatide trials.
A 2025 joint expert advisory suggests smaller, more frequent meals, and avoiding fatty or high-fibre foods during the first few days of treatment.
On the Zepbound label, nausea was reported by 25–29% on tirzepatide across doses vs 8% on placebo. Most nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea happened during dose escalation and decreased over time.

Safety:
If you have severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting, stop tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. It can be a sign of pancreatitis.
Signs of dehydration, or vomiting you can't keep up with? Contact your prescriber.
On insulin or a sulfonylurea? The label says your risk of low blood sugar may be higher. Eating much less is worth raising with your prescriber.
Kidney disease? Ask your clinician before raising your protein.
If you feel very unwell and can't reach anyone, use your local urgent care or emergency number.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.

Sources:
1. Zepbound Prescribing Information (rev. 28 Aug 2026): https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=487cd7e7-434c-4925-99fa-aa80b1cc776b
2. Zepbound Medication Guide (rev. 08/2026): https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-us-mg.pdf
3. Joint GLP-1 nutrition advisory, Obesity 2025: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/
4. NHS Dehydration (reviewed 01 May 2026): https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dehydration/

#tirzepatide #GLP1

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every number, quote and safety line against the primary sources, and the script is accurate.

**What matches the sources**
- **Zepbound label (Studies 1 and 2 pooled, both 72 weeks):** nausea 25/29/28% vs 8%, diarrhoea 19/21/23% vs 8%, constipation 17/14/11% vs 5%. Dyspepsia, eructation and GERD are also listed.
- **Mounjaro label:** nausea 12/15/18% vs 4%. The label is revised 27 Aug 2026.
- **Both labels:** the dose-escalation timing sentence, the gastric-emptying sentence ("largest after the first dose… diminishes over time"), and the low-blood-sugar caveat for insulin or sulfonylureas.
- **Medication Guide:** the lines on dehydration and kidney problems, drinking fluids, and belching, heartburn and indigestion as common side effects all match.
- **Joint advisory:** s19's quote is word for word from the advisory: "Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms." The advisory also supports the protein plus strength-training point.
- **NHS pages:**
  - Diarrhoea: "eat when you feel able to – it may help to avoid foods that are fatty or spicy" and "do not have fruit juice or fizzy drinks". Reviewed 21 Dec 2023.
  - Constipation: gradually increase fibre, drink fluids, a daily walk or run. Reviewed 26 Oct 2023.
  - Reflux: smaller meals, nothing 3–4 h before bed, raise the bed 10–20 cm, avoid tight waistbands, avoid trigger foods. Reviewed 20 Nov 2023.
  - Dehydration: the symptoms list. Reviewed 01 May 2026.

**Safety:** all the needed caveats are there: kidney disease and protein, fluid restriction, insulin or sulfonylureas, the pancreatitis stop-and-call line, the scoped don't-stop line, the emergency number for all four markets, and the prescriber line.

**Fixes before publishing:** five wording tweaks and two source-list fixes, all minor.
- Two "that's why" causal overstatements (s12, s13).
- One unsourced "commonly described" (s51).
- One cross-population comparison worded as a direct one (s14).
- One stat card that doesn't name its symptom (s39).
- One dehydration call threshold set too low (s36).
- Source list: the Medication Guide needs its own URL, and the Mounjaro label needs its exact revision date (27 Aug 2026).

These are precise and copy-pasteable. None of them changes the science.

issues.claim: "That's why meal size matters…" / "And it's why pace matters."
issues.problem: This states as fact that slower stomach emptying causes the meal-size and pace effects. The house rules ban "that's why". The label also says the delay shrinks over time, so it's only a plausible reason, not a proven one.
issues.fix: s12 narration: "That's one reason meal size can matter. A portion that felt normal before can feel like far too much, because the room fills before the queue clears." s13 narration: "Pace can matter too. Eating slowly gives you time to notice comfortably full before you've sailed past it." Change the on-screen text to "Pace can matter too".

issues.claim: "In the label's diabetes trials, nausea was lower: twelve to eighteen percent…"
issues.problem: This compares two different trial groups with different designs and lengths. It isn't a head-to-head result, and "was lower" suggests a direct comparison.
issues.fix: Narration: "A side note if you take Mounjaro for type two diabetes. In the label's diabetes trials, a different group of people, nausea was reported by twelve to eighteen percent across doses, versus four percent on placebo."

issues.problem: A muted viewer can't tell which side effect the number refers to.
No source backs "commonly". Sulfur burps aren't named on the label.
issues.fix: Narration: "You'll also hear some people describe sulfur burps, burps that smell like rotten eggs. They're not named on the label, and we won't guess at the cause." On-screen text: "Sulfur burps: not on the label"

thumbnail.reasoning:
All three are legible at phone size, use 4 words or fewer, keep the curiosity gap (none give away the answer), and the worried/queasy stomach face matches the mild-distress tone of each headline, so none trip the hard caps for emotion mismatch. 

Candidate #1 ("WHICH FOODS HELP?") directly echoes the title's own words ("Foods That May Help"), which triggers the repeats-the-title cap (ctr ≤ 5). It's also the least distinctive hook of the three — it just restates the video's premise as a question rather than adding a new angle.

Candidate #2 ("1 IN 4" / "Feel queasy. Why?") is a solid, credible curiosity hook with a concrete number, but "1 in 4" alone isn't specific to nausea or eating until you read the small subtext, so it's a notch less immediately gripping.

Candidate #0 ("DINNER LIKE A BRICK?") is the strongest: it's a vivid, specific, felt-problem image straight from the video's "you" scenario (a heavy meal sitting badly), it doesn't restate any title words, it keeps the full curiosity gap (no foods are named), and it pairs a visceral physical sensation with the worried stomach character's expression. This matches the growth playbook's preferred packaging (drug + felt problem + plain question) and is the most scroll-stopping of the three without being misleading.

▶ Watch next: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Side Effects: <SIDE_EFFECTS_URL>
Smaller meals, eaten slowly, and going easier on greasy food are commonly recommended habits, not results proven in tirzepatide trials.
A 2025 joint expert advisory suggests smaller, more frequent meals, and avoiding fatty or high-fibre foods during the first few days of treatment.
Zepbound label (2 pooled 72-week trials in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition): nausea 25–29% on tirzepatide across doses vs 8% on placebo. Most nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea happened during dose escalation and decreased over time.

Safety:
If you have severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting, stop tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. It can be a sign of pancreatitis.
Signs of dehydration, or vomiting you can't keep up with? Contact your prescriber.
On insulin or a sulfonylurea? The label says your risk of low blood sugar may be higher. Eating much less is worth raising with your prescriber.
Kidney disease? Ask your clinician before raising your protein.
If you feel very unwell and can't reach anyone, use your local urgent care or emergency number.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.
